packet-capture-act-1.title: Packet Capture CTF · Act I: The Signal

items.title: Digital Footprint
items.insight: A ban hides a subreddit from the live site but not from the Arctic Shift archive, and following its members to their new sub led to the flag post. Following the people instead of the place shows where a community moved.

items.title: Forgotten Repository
items.insight: Deleting a secret in a new commit doesn't remove it from git history. Always read the diffs, not just the latest files, and expect decoys when several flag-shaped strings appear.

items.title: Hidden Profile
items.insight: A CDX prefix query on twitter.com found archived tweets that the x.com lookup missed, and the id_ raw capture showed the flag tweet. For X/Twitter, search both x.com and twitter.com, use the CDX API with matchType=prefix to list every captured URL under a profile (including individual tweets), and add id_ to read the raw capture.

items.title: Last Breadcrumb
items.insight: Each pivot reuses the latest clue on a site already visited (hash > YouTube > Mastodon > paste > PGP keyserver > Mastodon > YouTube). The decoys (thisIsNotTheFlag, 0ld_k3ys) are labelled as wrong keys by the story itself, and the flag is split, so both halves must be joined before submitting.

items.title: Scattered Identities
items.insight: The sheet's owner email linked it to GitHub, Instagram and X, and the final step was emailing the owner with the turtle names, not searching. Every identity here is linked, not named: the metadata gives the email, the email gives GitHub, the username gives Instagram and X, and the rules on one platform (odd/even, 2-7) decode the list on another. The hints and bios said to contact the owner.

items.title: Silent Observer
items.insight: Each clue sat in an overlooked place (image metadata, an encoded tweet, a what3words address in an anonymous message) and ended at a cafe's phone number. The obvious leads (the face in the photo, the account's food posts) were decoys. The account's own "throwaway" tweets explained how to use each clue.

items.title: Treasure Hunt Time
items.insight: The metadata comment was a decoy, and the coordinates came from the file name as the what3words address treasure.hunt.trip. The hard part was formatting: DMS degrees.minutes, no signs, no space.

items.title: Under Construction
items.insight: The brief's details (blinking text, guestbooks, counters, a deliberate mass deletion) pointed to GeoCities, and Wikipedia pinned the deletion to 26 October 2009. Turn era-specific details (blinking text, guestbooks, visitor counters, "Under Construction") into a candidate, then pin the exact date with a primary source, watching for near-miss dates (the announcement date, or a regional spin-off that closed later).

packet-capture-act-2.title: Packet Capture CTF · Act II: The Breach

items.title: Forgotten Router
items.insight: The flag file /flag.txt was left readable at the web root, so one unauthenticated GET bypassed the whole login gate. The login and diagnostics CGI pages were a distraction: "a request that can finally end its misery" is literally one GET request to the file the firmware forgot to protect.

items.title: Internal Trouble
items.insight: The Is Website Down checker fetched URLs from the server side and its loopback denylist missed IPv6, so http://[::1]:3001 reached the internal dashboard. The internal monitor on port 3001 is only reachable from the server and is protected by a weak loopback denylist that matches IPv4 literals only. Reaching it as http://[::1]:3001 (or any hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1) bypasses the filter, and the dashboard screenshot carries the flag in its EXIF data.

packet-capture-act-3.title: Packet Capture CTF · Act III: The Echo

items.title: Deleted Doesn't Mean Gone
items.insight: Wiping the file table doesn't erase the data: carving by the PK signature found an intact ZIP at offset 12800 of the image. Signature-based carving (PK, %PDF, JPEG FFD8, etc.) finds intact files in unallocated space without any filesystem metadata.

items.title: Hidden Within
items.insight: The message was hidden in the least significant bit of the red channel only, so the usual RGB-interleaved extraction returned garbage. Test each colour channel's LSB on its own as well as interleaved.

items.title: Last Packet
items.insight: The flag was XORed with a per-packet key schedule and split across 9 ICMP pings sent out of order, and a known flag prefix exposed the keys. Reorder ICMP payloads by sequence number, not timestamp, and from the first keystream bytes you can work out the key schedule.

items.title: Memory Echoes
items.insight: Among nine identical-looking MFT records, one had an extra named data stream whose 35 bytes were single-byte XOR with key 0x3C. Look for the structural outlier. Short opaque blobs are often single-byte XOR, so brute-forcing all 256 keys is quick to try. The flag text ("echo in the registry") matches the challenge story.

items.title: Registry Secrets
items.insight: The flag was split across two hex blocks in cirt_agent.exe's environment and XORed with MEM_XOR_SEED=90 (0x5A) from the dump's config line. Tie the process list to network activity first: the process talking to a known-bad port is the one whose data matters. Read "90" as decimal (0x5A), not hex.

items.title: USB Secrets
items.insight: One USBSTOR device had a serial split into 8-character hex chunks that decode to PacketCapture{DEVICE_HISTORY}. Knowing what a normal artifact looks like (vendor, product, rev, serial) makes the field that breaks the pattern stand out. Hex that starts with 50 61 63 6B is "Pack", the start of the flag format.

items.title: Emanation
items.insight: Both countermeasures leaked their own secret: the delay showed up as a marker spike to align on, and the mask leaked in its own sample, so a centered product cancelled it. A first-order mask only raises the attack to second order. It stops being cheap only when the shares are not separately observable, or with higher-order masking plus real jitter.

items.title: The Keywheel
items.insight: Any 624 consecutive MT19937 outputs reveal the whole state, and the twist runs backward as easily as forward, so keys from before the recorded window were exposed too. Deriving key material straight from a non-cryptographic PRNG breaks both forward and backward secrecy.

items.title: The Signet
items.insight: Nonces that step by a fixed stride make every ECDSA signature a linear equation in the private key, start and stride, so three signatures solve for the key and the rest verify it.

items.title: Watchword
items.insight: AES-GCM nonce reuse breaks the authenticator, not just confidentiality: tags under one nonce share H and S, so a polynomial GCD over GF(2^128) recovers both without the AES key. Once S is known, anything keyed off that same per-nonce value falls too, here a second payload encrypted under E_K(J0).

items.title: Briefing for One
items.insight: The shortcut's own command line held the full recipe, so I rebuilt its MachineGuid-keyed HMAC password and carved its WebDAV 7z from the capture without running anything. The hashes the shortcut embeds prove the reconstruction is byte-exact, and the DLL is never loaded.

items.title: Ghost in the Historian
items.insight: The deleted encryptor seeds a xorshift32 XOR keystream from time ^ pid, and it stamped that time into every .enc mtime and logged the pid, so the key was sitting on disk. Because the keystream is pure XOR, decryption is the same routine as encryption. The state carries between files, so the decrypt order has to be the encryptor's scandir order, not whatever order a listing returns.

items.title: Interlock Witness
items.insight: The policy judges each Modbus write on the state just before its response, so I replayed the capture in wire order and applied each accepted write only after its response. Checking every response against its request (transaction, protocol, unit and function match, FC16 address and quantity echo, FC03 byte count) is what separates a write the controller accepted from one the client merely sent. Reproducing the policy's own counts (8 ineligible writes, 5 of them prerequisite-state) showed the classification was right before the hash was taken.

items.title: Last Buffer
items.insight: Both Vim swap files restored cleanly, so I picked the real one by the PID in its header, which matched the shell that died on pts/4 inside the crash window. The base-file hash, matching what that shell's own sha256sum printed, confirmed it, because the drill revision looks just as plausible by content alone.

items.title: Last Commit
items.insight: The SQLite WAL kept every committed state, so replaying it commit by commit gave the export exactly as it stood when LR-731 flipped to COMPLETED at frame 5. Only a frame with a non-zero database size commits the page images before it, and the replay has to stop at the job's commit, because the tampering was undone two commits later.

items.title: Operation Dawn - The Medic's Phone
items.insight: Withdrawing the message only rewrote the live SQLite row, while the write-ahead log still held an older page with the original deflated text. Parsing the WAL by hand and inflating the protobuf bodies brought it back.

items.title: Ortelia VDR Carving
items.insight: The chip-off PNG was split into four sector runs, and the IDAT chunk's own length and CRC32 told me how many sectors were missing and which order was right. Carving from the header to the end of the data gives a file that opens but is truncated, and the zero-sector gaps at 21, 34, 42 and 43 were the clue that it was split.

items.title: Polyglot Requiem
items.insight: The flag was a 36-byte blob in a deleted SQLite cell inside a ZIP appended after a PNG's IEND, XORed with SHA-256 of the PNG's reversed Provenance tag and a git commit time. Each innocent-looking layer (an unreachable commit, a polyglot icon, an unlinked cell) hid one piece, and the pieces only meet in that key derivation. The curl-to-shell line was a reason to read the history, not to run it.

items.title: Recon Plate
items.insight: Bits 0 and 1 each held a separate gzip and tar message, and the plain LSB layer was a drill decoy, so the real code 3F8C21 only appeared in bit plane 1. The clue was that the two planes started almost identically, then diverged.

items.title: Redline
items.insight: Word keeps deleted text inside document.xml as w:del runs, so the approved authorization was never gone, just marked deleted, while a forged one was inserted in its place by s.kessler.

items.title: Relay Capture
items.insight: The editor saved the cropped PNG over the original without truncating it, so the old compressed rows sat after IEND and inflated again once I found the right bit offset.

items.title: Shadow-Dispatch
items.insight: A poisoned Lambda layer shipped a hash-based, unchecked .pyc that did not match its clean .py, and it leaked SSM secrets 2 bytes at a time through the telemetry correlation field. Nothing in the function code changed, and each chunk was encrypted with a key derived from the request ID.

items.title: Silent Breaker
items.insight: A rogue SS7 peer harvested SMS routing to intercept the one OT-VPN user's OTP, then an IEC-104 single command tripped the breaker while the historian showed a frozen current. No single source tells the whole story: the telecom feed gives the who, RADIUS the how, the pcap the what and the historian the cover-up, and each step needed the previous step's output to be trusted.

items.title: Telltale
items.insight: The status LED was Manchester-keyed at 1000 bit/s, far too fast for the eye to see, so a photodiode sampled at 48 kHz could read the exfiltrated flag straight off it. A steady-looking status LED is not a quiet output.

items.title: The Capability Ghost
items.insight: The seal key sat in plain metadata, the TAG in a PAX user xattr and the EPOCH in a journal field, and hc-probe's own help text spelled out the cipher, so the marker unseals statically without root.

items.title: The Layer That Wouldn't Die
items.insight: The seal was keyed on the marker as it stood at the end of layer 3, so the rev-A value still stored in layer 2 unseals it, while the later rev-B overwrite and the layer-5 whiteout are decoys. A file deleted in a later layer is still stored in the layer that created it.

items.title: Tone Burst
items.insight: The audio is 50-baud binary FSK (2 kHz = 1, 1 kHz = 0), and a 32-bit 1010 preamble plus an HDLC-style 0x7E flag marks exactly where the ASCII payload starts. Looking for the sync pattern first beats guessing the byte alignment.

items.title: Water Hammer Reconciliation
items.insight: Only an FC16 write whose echo is followed by a matching FC3 readback counts as confirmed state, so the exception and unanswered writes drop out and exactly 64 snapshots remain. An acknowledgement is not state, and reassembling TCP before framing Modbus keeps packet boundaries from creating false events.

items.title: Dispatch Authenticator
items.insight: With a batch of one, a fully connected first layer with a bias leaks its input exactly, since dividing a weight-gradient row by its bias gradient gives x. In federated learning, sharing only gradients is not a privacy guarantee. Bigger models need an optimisation attack (Deep Leakage from Gradients, Zhu et al. 2019) instead of a division, but the leak is the same.

items.title: Lattice
items.insight: A cipher built only from invertible steps, with seeds and constants published in its own source, can be decrypted by reversing each round, so leaving out the decrypt routine protected nothing. The inverse is a mechanical reversal, and the "preimage" framing is a red herring: this is a cipher keyed only on paper, so recovering SECRET is plain decryption, not a hash preimage.

items.title: Operation Dawn - The Cipher Lock
items.insight: A comparison that runs the secret through an S-box leaks the secret's Hamming weight in power, one byte at a time. Because each code byte is checked independently, the search is 47 x 256 guesses, not 256^47. Known entered codes plus recorded traces are all an attacker needs, and the "no hardware required" note means the corpus already contains the leakage, so this is a pure data attack.

items.title: Warden
items.insight: An audit hook is a deny-list over a fixed set of instrumented operations, not a capability sandbox. It hears opens, imports, execs and subprocess spawns, but it is deaf to operations that need no OS interaction, such as attribute access, reading the environment and writing to a file descriptor. The whole exploit lives in that blind spot: walk the class graph to the already-loaded os module and read the secret straight out of the environment. Emptying builtins and allowing only attribute reads looks locked down but leaves the whole silent-computation surface open.

items.title: Ghost Signal
items.insight: The attacker's IMSI was the only malformed 15-digit one and the one value present in SS7, Diameter and billing, so cross-referencing the three files exposed the chain. Confirming it in both captures before trusting the billing record proves the thread, and sorting the billing events pins the first anomalous timestamp.

items.title: Grid-Watch
items.insight: The link refuses unsigned and replayed commands, but the note hands over the exact HKDF that builds the provisioning key, and every input to it is recoverable from the evidence: the serial from a STATUSTEXT, the epoch by calibrating the RTC ticks, and the nonce from the connect banner. Re-signing is legitimate per the protocol, so the only real work is getting the epoch byte-exact (hence the exact-arithmetic calibration) and keeping signing timestamps current so each frame is accepted.

items.title: Severed Link
items.insight: Signing only buys authenticity while the key is secret, and the operator distributed the new key over the very channel it protects, where it was recorded. Capturing the key beats breaking the crypto, since no cryptographic weakness is needed, just the leaked 32 bytes. The gateway's replay protection (monotonic, current timestamps) and heartbeat-first handshake work correctly and are irrelevant once the key is in the attacker's hands, because they just sign fresh frames like the real operator.

items.title: Silent Orbit
items.insight: The suppressed record is fully determined by the relay's published state machine. Strict adherence to the rules (APID and flag filtering, tuple match, Metadata before data, snapshot at the first valid EOF, and the CFDP header-length convention) yields the exact NAK PDU, and the decoy transaction and out-of-state PDUs are what make a naive parser get it wrong.

items.title: Echo Chamber
items.insight: A %s echo is a leak oracle whenever you can control where its NUL terminator falls - overwriting one known zero byte turns "harmless echo" into an arbitrary adjacent-memory read, and repeating it peels the canary, the stack cookie's neighbours, the PIE return and (via an rbp pivot back into the same printf) a libc pointer. When the only gadget is leave;ret, you still win by pivoting rbp/rsp into a buffer whose address you just leaked and ROPing from there in a second stage. A single 0x20-byte overflow is enough.

items.title: Command Authority
items.insight: Data appended after the JPEG end marker held the archive password, and the verifier's restricted clearance was stored XORed with 0x41, so one XOR scan recovered it without running the program. The nested archive provided the verifier, and static analysis of its embedded comparison data revealed the value.

items.title: Fence Shift
items.insight: A queue acknowledgement is not proof the controller accepted the reposition, so I drove the state timeline from the aircraft's matching parameter confirmation and took the predicate from the binary. The exact controller predicate has to be recovered from the binary rather than inferred from the route manager's response.

items.title: Operation Dawn - Radio Recovery
items.insight: Each layer named its successor, so the msgcat adler32 dictid unlocked rootfs and the newer env copy's MAC XORed with the token gave the flag. The DWFW CRCs showed the four blobs were intact, the init script spelled out the XOR, and the env's flag byte plus recovery state told me which of the two MACs was live.

items.title: Apogee
items.note: Supply-chain, ZIP duplicate-name + symlink parser-differential writes into a write-protected store
items.insight: A parser differential -- the verifier and the extractor disagreed about the same bytes. ZIP permits duplicate entry names and carries unix symlink modes; the verifier hashed the file resolved by name while extract-zip created a same-named symlink first and wrote the file through it, out of the sandbox and into the write-protected store. Validation on one interpretation, side effects on another = a confused-deputy write. "Write-protected" at the app layer is meaningless when a library writes as the trusted pipeline process. Defensive takeaways (supply-chain / GRC angle): - Validate and extract the EXACT same entry/bytes. Resolve names identically on both sides, reject archives with - Treat archive symlinks (and unix modes) as hostile. Extract with symlinks disabled / O_NOFOLLOW, resolve each - Constrain writers by the OS, not by convention: run extraction as an unprivileged user that cannot write the - Make the audit trail authoritative on content, not just on "an accepted delivery occurred": compare the written

items.title: Corridor Transit Gate
items.insight: The gateway and the backend disagree on what a path means. The gateway's allow/deny ran on a slightly different normalization of the URL than the backend's router used to dispatch it. "..%2f" is the sweet spot: the gateway doesn't decode %2f (so it never sees the /internal/ segment and allows the request), but the backend does decode and collapse it (so it routes straight to the emergency-override handler). The front-end JS handed over the exact endpoint and body; the whole challenge was defeating that one boundary control.

items.title: Cutover
items.insight: Two bugs stacked on one trust boundary. (1) A parser differential — flatted 3.4.1 treats a value string as an index into its own cell array, so "__proto__" yields a live reference to Array.prototype, and a shallow merge onto it becomes global prototype pollution even though the identical JSON is harmless. Storing authorization grants in an Array indexed by action name (`grants[action]`) is what turns that pollution into a privilege escalation. (2) A validator/parser mismatch — the risk gateway recognises only the bare-integer number grammar and "defers" anything else, while the engine parses full RFC 8259, so `3.11e7` means "under review" to the screen and "31,100,000" to the engine.

items.title: Helioform Relay
items.insight: Defence-in-depth that is never enforced is decoration. An "agent-only" subprotocol with no auth, a dial primitive that is loopback SSRF, secrets a verifier signs with sitting in a reachable dotenv, a MAC key only as safe as every service that can read it, and os.path.join(root, attacker) that an absolute path walks straight out of -- each is routine, and chained they go from an inert bench to code execution as the relay user.

items.title: Interlock
items.insight: Four components each parse the same bytes differently — fast-uri vs WHATWG for the host, NFKC vs plain casefold for the identity, raw vs normalized for the path. The attacker lives in every gap: a string that looks safe to the checker and dangerous to the executor. The fix is parser unanimity — authorize on, and act on, the exact same canonical value.

items.title: Key Custody
items.insight: Never let attacker-controlled token metadata select the verification key. `kid` picked the HMAC secret, and the secret was a publicly downloadable file — so the attacker holds the key and can mint any token. Two failures had to line up: a `kid` resolved as a filesystem path (with `..` traversal), and a key source that is not actually secret. Either alone is bad; together they are a full admin forge.

items.title: Operation Dawn - The Dispatch Console
items.insight: The sanitiser and WAF only guarded the front door (the /post write and the /dispatches read). The /digest report re-used the stored callsign in a concatenated query, so a value that was stored safely became a SQL injection the second time it was read — classic second-order, invisible to the request-time WAF.

items.title: Operation Dawn - The Standing Order
items.insight: Two classic bugs chained. (1) A secret-prefix SHA-1 MAC (SHA1(secret||data)) is forgeable via length extension without the secret — you can append attacker data and still produce a valid tag; here that flips role=operator to role=admin. (2) The SSRF guard was a string blacklist of loopback spellings, so an alternate encoding of the same address (decimal 2130706433) reaches 127.0.0.1 anyway.

items.title: Two-Key Turn
items.insight: The two-person rule is an invariant ("2 distinct officers"), and the server enforced it with a read-check-write sequence that was not atomic. Under concurrency the gap between "check the caller is a new officer" and "commit the approval record" lets a single officer's parallel requests each pass the check before any of them writes, so one credential satisfies a rule that requires two. The 8-second pending window just made the race wide and comfortable.

items.title: Vesper Quay Board
items.insight: Two JSON parsers, one request. Go's encoding/json folds key case and takes the last duplicate; Python's json is exact and case-sensitive. The desk validated the UPPER-case keys while the quay executed the lower-case ones — a confused-deputy that turns a "safe" validation into attacker-chosen code on the box that holds the signing key. From there the signature is genuine, so the forged-warrant defense (requiring a station signature) is satisfied by the station itself.

QWERTZ-98 salting multiplies the message by a number built from the password, so the password's prime factors survive in the ciphertext and trial division reveals it with no wordlist. Real ciphers mix the key and data so that nothing about the key can be read back out of the output. Obscure formats and stacked encodings add effort, not security.

items.title: Soeder Swim
items.insight: The politician's Instagram caption plus one reverse image search found the exact pool in a single hop, because the pool's own Instagram had reposted the photo. The flag even nods to it: "Sweet Caroline" is 1. FC Nürnberg's stadium anthem. Skipping the decoy panorama left the effort for the real-world location.

items.title: Journey
items.insight: Nine stacked layers were only keyless transforms or keys stored next to the data, so reading each decoder and skipping the decoy branches solved it without running anything. The Java layer's AES key sat beside the ciphertext. The skill this trains is reverse engineering: reading unfamiliar languages, separating the live code path from decoys, and reimplementing a decoder safely instead of running untrusted code. That is the same habit as triaging a malware dropper chain.

items.title: Cluck Cluck
items.insight: The flag was in the one place a normal run never reaches, the code the program always jumps over. It sat behind three layers of misdirection: audible clucks that look like a cipher but are a formula, an LSB payload that looks like a meaningless repeating pattern but is source code, and a program whose output says "nothing suspicious".

items.title: Suspicious Numbers
items.insight: Every number was 1337 times an atomic number, so dividing by 1337 and reading the element symbols as letters spelled the hidden sentence.

items.title: TNS2
items.insight: The readable flag in the file is a decoy, and the real one is split between line segments drawn as letters and two text fragments that fill the gaps in them. It only appears when the figure is rendered and the gaps are matched to the text positions. If a platform rejects it, the likeliest alternate readings are fl or Fl for fL, and tns or TnS for tnS.

items.title: Escaped
items.insight: A raw 0xBF byte before the quote swallowed the escaper's 0x5C backslash on a multibyte connection, so the quote survived and broke out of the SQL string. Escaping is not parameterizing, and the flag says so: 0x5C is not always a backslash. addslashes and mysqli_real_escape_string prepend 0x5C to a quote, but on a multibyte connection (GBK and similar) a lead byte can consume that 0x5C, so the quote survives.

items.title: SQL Injection
items.insight: A raw 0xBF byte before the quote swallowed the escaper's 0x5C backslash on a multibyte connection, so the quote survived and broke out of the SQL string. Escaping is not parameterizing, and the flag says so: 0x5C is not always a backslash. addslashes and mysqli_real_escape_string prepend 0x5C to a quote, but on a multibyte connection (GBK and similar) a lead byte can consume that 0x5C, so the quote survives.
